description_full: Cousins Properties Incorporated is a fully integrated, self-administered, and self-managed real estate investment trust (REIT). The Company is acting through its operating partnership, Cousins Properties LP, primarily invests in Class A office buildings located in high-growth Sun Belt markets. Founded in 1958, Cousins creates shareholder value through its extensive expertise in the development, acquisition, leasing, and management of high-quality real estate assets. The Company has a comprehensive strategy based on a simple platform, trophy assets, and opportunistic investments. Cousins Properties was founded in 1958 and is incorporated in Georgia.
ceo_bio: Mr. Michael Colin Connolly | President, CEO & Director | Age 48 | Compensation: $2.5M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 351 people. Revenue per employee of $2.8M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 16%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $385K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $47K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Cousins Properties Incorporated is a mid-cap real estate business with a $4.9B market cap on $994M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +4.6pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $135M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.93× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.2×.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 68% operating margin runs 45pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.40x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 13% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market.
About $39.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash, 46% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 36% below its DCF fair value of $46.32, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 40%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $27.69 to $76.18 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 12.9 vs 16.3, richer on P/E 328.9 vs 23.6 and P/FCF 36.1 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 25% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $33.27 on average, 12% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.48).
It converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 14%.
ROE of 1% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.1x net debt to EBITDA ($5.7M of cash against $3.3B of debt), with interest covered 4.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.06 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.2% over 3 years, 6.1% over 5 years and 10.0% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 30%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue up 12% and FFO growth of 2.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (26.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (1.0%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 4.4% a year to shareholders (4.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 2.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 1422% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 11.3% of the float, 8.9 days to cover.
people: With about 351 employees, each generates about $2.8M of revenue, 1.2x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 15.8% a year.
That works out to $385K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
